original_value: AbstractIn this paper, an artificial potential field based navigational controller has been developed for motion planning of humanoid robots. Here, NAO robots are used as the humanoid platform using the underlying principles of potential field based method. The movement of the robot is considered to be under a negative gradient scheme by the combined effect of attractive and repulsive forces generated due to target and obstacles, respectively. The working of the controller is tested in a V‐REP simulation platform, and the simulation results are validated through a real‐time experimental set‐up developed under laboratory conditions. Here, the navigation of both single and multiple humanoids has been attempted. For avoiding intercollision among multiple humanoids during their navigation in a common platform, a Petri‐Net control scheme has been proposed. The results obtained from both the simulation and experimental platforms are compared against each other with a good agreement between them having minimal percentage of deviations. Finally, the proposed controller is also evaluated against another existing navigational model, and a significant performance improvement has been observed.

result.paraphrase: This paper presents an artificial-potential-field-based navigation controller for humanoid robot motion planning. NAO robots serve as the humanoid platform, and the controller follows potential-field principles, with robot motion modeled as a negative-gradient process driven by attractive forces from the goal and repulsive forces from obstacles. Its performance is examined in V-REP simulation and then confirmed through a real-time laboratory experimental setup. Navigation is attempted for both single and multiple humanoid robots. To prevent intercollision among multiple humanoids moving on a shared platform, a Petri net control scheme is proposed. The simulation and experimental outcomes agree closely, with only minimal percentage deviations. The proposed controller is also compared with another existing navigation model, showing significant performance improvement.
